segments: and censured him and blamed him because he made peace with Saladin.
And that lord of Mosul gathered about twenty thousand horsemen,
and he came to Aleppo.
And he released the nobles of the Franks who had been imprisoned there for a long time:
and he sold the Count of Tripoli for eighty thousand dinars,
and Joscelin the son of Joscelin for fifty [thousand],
and the Prince of Antioch for one hundred and twenty [thousand].
And he made them swear that they would be helpers at all times.
And Saladin again sent to Egypt and gathered his forces.
And they all met between Aleppo and Hama,
at a place called Gubbay Turkmanaye (the Cisterns of the Turkmens),
and they engaged one another.
And Saladin defeated the people of Aleppo and Mosul a second time,
and he put them to flight.
And he gained control over their tents and plundered their baggage,
and he found in them a multitude of birds: turtledoves, pigeons, parrots and parakeets {OCR?} in cages,
and a hundred wanton singing-girls.
And he called one of the chamberlains and sent him as an envoy to Sayf al-Din,
and with him those cages.
And he said to him:
"Go, greet Sayf al-Din on my behalf, and say to him:
'Return to your childhood by playing with your birds,
for they are beautiful,
and they do not bring one into danger at all.'"
And the Mosulite nobles whom he had captured—
among whom was Fakhr al-Din Abd al-Masih—
he clothed,
and gave them provisions and gifts,
and sent them away in peace.
And while leaving Aleppo in the middle,
he crossed over and encamped against the fortress of Buza'ah and captured it.
And from there he came to Mabbug (Hierapolis),
and he took possession of it as well,
and found in its fortress treasure to the amount of three hundred thousand dinars.
And he came against 'Azaz,
and in the space of forty days he captured it.
And in that same year,
which is 1487,
1487 of the Greeks [1176 AD],
Manuel, the emperor of the Greeks, went out,
and built two cities on the border of the Turks,
and placed forces in them.
And they greatly oppressed the house of Qilij Arslan,
for the reason that the emperor was demanding from the Sultan that he restore to the house of Danishmand their lands,
and he was not willing.
Therefore the emperor sent thirty thousand Greek horsemen [under] the command of {OCR?} Dhu'l-Nun the Turkmen, the son of Danishmand,
and they encamped against Neocaesarea.
